text: Narendra Krishna Karmarkar, born in 1956, is an Indian mathematician who developed Karmarkar's algorithm. He is listed as an ISI highly cited researcher. He invented one of the first provably polynomial time algorithms for linear programming, known as an interior point method, which is a cornerstone in the field. He published this result in 1984 while working at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey. Karmarkar earned his B.Tech. in electrical engineering from IIT Bombay in 1978, an M.S. from the California Institute of Technology in 1979, and a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of California, Berkeley in 1983 under Richard M. Karp. He served as a post-doctoral research fellow at IBM Research (1983), Member of Technical Staff and fellow at the Mathematical Sciences Research Center, AT&T Bell Laboratories (1983–1998), professor of mathematics at M.I.T. (1991), at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton (1996), and Homi Bhabha Chair Professor at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai from 1998 to 2005. He was the scientific advisor to the chairman of the TATA group from 2006 to 2007, during which time he was funded by Ratan Tata to scale up the supercomputer he designed and prototyped at TIFR. The scaled-up model outperformed a supercomputer in Japan at the time and achieved India's best-ever ranking in supercomputing. He was the founding director of the Computational Research Labs in Pune, where this scaling-up work took place. He continues to work on a new architecture for supercomputing based on concepts from finite geometry, particularly projective geometry over finite fields. Karmarkar's algorithm solves linear programming problems in polynomial time, represented by a set of linear constraints and variables. The traditional approach involved treating the problem as a high-dimensional solid with vertices and moving from vertex to vertex, whereas Karmarkar's method traverses through the solid, significantly reducing solution time. For instance, in a communications network optimization problem, solution time dropped from weeks to days, enabling faster business and policy decisions. His algorithm has inspired the development of several interior-point methods, some of which are used in current linear-programming solvers.
